title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: a garland tossed to an elephant, and the goddess of fortune leaves the worlds
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Durga's fierce form as Kali, dancing until Shiva lay still in her path. Did you try being the still one when something was spinning? Today, a quieter goddess, and a story about losing her. Day one thousand seventy-five.

Indra, king of the gods, is riding his great white elephant, feeling fine about himself. On the road he meets a sage, Durvasa, known for his temper. The sage is wandering in a wild, ecstatic state, a garland of heavenly flowers on his own head. He takes it off and throws it up to the king. Indra catches it. And without really looking at it, he hangs it on the elephant's head. The elephant smells the flowers, takes the garland in its trunk, and throws it on the ground. That small careless moment is where today's story begins, with the goddess Lakshmi, and the day she left.
screen: `A SAGE OFFERS A GARLAND.` → `THE KING HANDS IT TO HIS ELEPHANT.` → `THE GARLAND HITS THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The sage sees his garland in the dirt, and his temper breaks. In the Vishnu Purana's telling, he curses Indra: since the king is so swollen with his fortune, his fortune will leave him. And it does. Shri, the goddess of fortune and prosperity, also called Lakshmi, departs from the three worlds. What happens next is quietly frightening. Nobody attacks. Nothing explodes. Things just go dim. In the Purana's description, the plants wither, people stop offering and giving, the gods lose their strength, and the demons start winning. All because one goddess is gone. So who is Lakshmi as a character? She isn't a warrior like Durga, and she isn't wild like Kali. She is the goddess of everything going well: the full granary, the lamp lit, the house where people are generous. In the text her leaving is the sage's curse at work, but some retellers draw a trait from it: she doesn't stay where she isn't honored. She isn't cruel about it. She simply isn't there anymore, and suddenly everyone notices what she was holding together. Some teachers draw a plain lesson from it. Fortune follows care, and it slips away from arrogance. A gift tossed aside, a blessing taken for granted, and the shine goes out of things. And the story doesn't end in the dark. To bring her back, the gods will have to do something enormous, and they'll have to do it together with their enemies. That's tomorrow: the churning of the ocean, and Lakshmi rising from it. Today, just sit with the strange quiet of a world she has left.
screen: `THE SAGE CURSES THE PROUD KING.` · `SHRI LEAVES THE THREE WORLDS.` · `NOTHING EXPLODES; THINGS GO DIM.` · then, large: `SHE DOESN'T STAY WHERE SHE ISN'T HONORED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: look at one garland. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one good thing in your life that you've stopped noticing: a friend who always texts back, a body that works, a warm room, a meal that simply appears. Something you'd only miss if it were gone. Hold it the way Indra should have held the garland: really look at it. Let a little gratitude rise, without forcing it. If you pray, you can offer thanks to Lakshmi or to God. If you don't, just notice. The bell holds the time.
Durga. The name over this run of five goddesses; today, the run turns to Lakshmi, whose leaving dims the worlds. Today's word.

Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Today, pick up one garland you've been tossing aside, and say thank you for it, out loud. Tomorrow, Lakshmi rises from the ocean. Day one thousand seventy-five.

howItsDone: Hindus honor Lakshmi in homes and shops, especially at Diwali, and some families keep the house clean and lamps lit in the hope that she will feel welcome and stay.

fork.setup: you're Indra, riding your elephant. a sage with a famous temper throws you a garland. what does the story say you do?
options: drop it onto the elephant's head
fork.reveal: Indra drops it on the elephant, which throws it to the ground. Durvasa curses him, and Shri, fortune herself, leaves the three worlds.

original.note: Sanskrit: Shri, fortune, prosperity, radiance; in the Vishnu Purana's story, the goddess who leaves the worlds.

notes: Paraphrased from Vishnu Purana 1.9 (Wilson 1840 exists in the public domain but is not on the validator's list; nothing quoted). Confirm details: Durvasa in a good mood; Indra places the garland on Airavata's head; the elephant throws it down; the curse ties to Indra's pride in his prosperity; effects (plants wither, sacrifices cease, gods weaken, demons advance).
'She doesn't stay where she isn't honored' is drawn as a character trait from this story; in the text the departure is the effect of Durvasa's curse. Keeper may prefer stating that more strictly.
'Some teachers draw a plain lesson: fortune follows care' is attributed, not asserted.
The churning (Lakshmi's return) is held for 1076.

Editor pass: Vishnu Purana 1.9 has Durvasa under a vow of madness, wearing the garland and throwing it to Indra, not 'in a good mood' offering a gift; hook, match and fork corrected. 'Her clearest trait' (superlative) reframed: the departure is the curse's effect, and the trait is offered as some retellers' reading.
